newsitem.title: USA: Inhaling heroin causes brain damage, says U.S. study.
newsitem.headline: Inhaling heroin causes brain damage, says U.S. study.

text.p: Inhaling heroin vapour, a practice known as "chasing the dragon," can severely damage parts of the brain responsible for movement, doctors warned in a study published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
Three researchers at the Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons in New York said they had treated two patients for the problem.

One was a 21-year-old woman whose body movements had become slow and shaky. Two weeks after being admitted to the hospital, the condition left her mute, nearly quadriplegic, and unable to stand or sit. A brain biopsy found that some of her white matter was deteriorating.

In the second case, a 40-year-old musician who had joined the woman in inhaling heroin vapour every day for two weeks discovered that he was bumping into furniture and having trouble playing the drums, even though he had stopped inhaling the heroin two weeks earlier.
He had slurred speech, erratic eye movements and could not move his body properly. His brain showed similar abnormalities.
Although similar reports have appeared in Europe, these are apparently the first two publicised cases in the United States, according to the Columbia group, led by Dr. Arnold R. Kriegstein.

"Chasing the dragon," the researchers said, "has no known treatment and a mortality rate of 25 percent." They said it was "gaining popularity among drug abusers in the United States as a means of ingesting heroin that averts the risk of exposure to HIV."
Addicts involved in the practice might be avoiding the AIDS virus but were trading it off for another big risk, the doctors said.
